text.en: The nations' hatred is itself a sign of their recognition: they ignore other peoples' boasts but hate the Jews because, deep down, they know the Jewish claim to chosenness is true.
Envy and hatred go together, as the Torah describes Yosef's brothers first envying him and then hating him.
Hitler's attack on Talmud learners shows that even the enemy understood that Torah is what keeps the Jews alive, and the greater quantity of Torah after the war shows that he failed.
The decline in the quality of Torah is not Hitler's doing but the natural result of each generation's greater distance from Sinai, the fountain, until the new fountain of the days of Moshiach.
Spain's fall into insignificance after the Jews left, compared with Eretz Yisrael appearing daily on the front page, illustrates how the Jews drive the importance of the nations they live among.
Just as the generation raised on the mann saw bread growing from the ground as a great wonder, the survival of the Jews is a wonder that goes unnoticed only because it is familiar.
The Mashgiach reads the land's desolation in golus and its blossoming on the Jews' return as one prophecy: the land refuses to produce for anyone but its own people.
The avodah zarah in Tanach is not evidence that Yidden abandoned the Torah; it was a yetzer hara as real as the pull of arayos or money today, which can trip even a scrupulously observant Jew.
The yetzer hara for avodah zarah did not disappear but changed its form, and today it is the drive for riches.
Leaving Yiddishkeit to escape persecution did not help: the destruction began in Germany where the abandonment began, and Hitler counted even converted families as Jews.
The Torah's prophecies are two contradictory predictions, a small, hated nation and an eternal one; foretelling both together is something only the Creator could do.
The Megillah is a miniature of Jewish history: its scattered details make sense only at the end, just as everything in world history serves one purpose, the Geulah of Klal Yisroel.

The fact that the same Chumash and Gemara serve a child, a lifelong scholar and every generation back to Moshe Rabbeinu, unlike any secular textbook, is itself a visible miracle showing that Torah comes from heaven.
The Torah calls idolatry by the unusual name 'eiker' only where a Jew is sold to it, because there it voices Hashem's protest: the idolatry will be uprooted so that the Jew is not.
The slave's descending levels mirror Mitzrayim: Hashem lets a person sink by his own choice, but cuts the time short before the point of no return, as He took the Jews out at the forty-ninth gate.
The redemptions of the sold Jew follow the order of Shemoneh Esrei: first the uprooting of heresy, then redemption through attaching to a tzaddik, then Moshiach ben David hinted in 'dodo'.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a Yovel of return: the word contains Shabbos, which means return, and on it heaven comes down to a person instead of his having to rise to it.
Rus returned from the field of Moav to Beis Lechem Yehudah, whose initial letters spell Yovel, which is why her story belongs to Shavuos.
Yovel means both a shofar and a stream, and the two meanings meet: with the shofar of redemption a Jew's roots are replanted by the stream of Torah.
The Mashgiach reads 'asher tikre'u osam' not only as Jews fixing the moadim but as Jews being the moadim themselves, each in his place in the calendar.
Because melacha comes from the 39 curses after the sin, Shabbos, which is blessing, has no place for it; a talmid chacham who is Shabbos is likewise freed from labor by those who are 'weekdays'.
Tisha B'Av is the one moed absent from Emor, because it is a moed that turned sour, like a gifted boy who strayed, waiting to be restored when Moshiach comes.
Rashi's two explanations of the ben ish Mitzri are one: refused a place in Dan's camp, he denied that the lowly tribe's challah, Hashem's love for it, stays fresh.
Each challah being baked separately shows that even Dan has its own individual importance before Hashem.
The Gemara's reading of 'yeshno' as 'grown old' makes Haman's claim the same as the ben ish Mitzri's, which is why this parsha belongs with Purim.
Moshe forgot what he did with the surplus silver because its donors were 'forgotten' souls outside the Mishkan, and a person's money, an extension of his soul, shares his fate.
The word nisayon means both a test and raising up, like a banner; a test exists to promote, and after ten tests Avraham 'graduated'.
The akeida was harder than the furnace of Ur Kasdim because there Avraham felt Hashem near, while at the akeida Hashem seemed far and Avraham had to act against his own understanding.
Eikev, the heel, is the least sensitive part of the body; the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha is in the dark and insensitive, and that is its test.
The rejected Jews are like the crowns on the letters: outside the letter itself, yet expounded by Rabbi Akiva, and they can express nuances of holiness that the letters alone do not.
The hooks are called vavim because a vav connects: the surplus Jews may be outside, but they are connected, and their hooks were crowned.
Unlike Yom Kippur, where one must go up, Purim comes down to the Jew; if it made non-Jews into Jews it can make a Jew a better Jew.
The Midrash reads 'megurei' in all three of its meanings at once, each explaining the others: Yitzchak made converts by merely dwelling in the land, and did it that way because his midah was fear.
Because Yitzchak's kiruv was hidden, the Torah tells it in a hidden way, by an innocent word, since the Torah is the blueprint of what happens in the world.
The three parts of a candle, ner, pesilah and shemen, spell nefesh, the bodily soul that holds the heavenly flame down on earth.

The halachos of the Chanukah light, in the public domain, at the left of the door, below ten tefachim, in the long nights of Teves, all place it in Esav's territory, showing that on Chanukah the Shechinah goes down to the distant.
Yosef's dream of the sun, moon and stars bowing to him is the picture of a Jew stooping to light the Chanukah candle, and Yaakov's 'shall we come down?' was an exclamation, not a question.
The letters of 'choshech', the darkness that stands for Yavan, rearranged spell 'shikchah', forgetting, since Yavan's aim was to make Jews forget the Torah.
The hatred of the nations is not something to be explained away; like the hatred between animals it is instinctive, and it serves as a preservative that keeps Jews from mixing with them.
The Jewish state, meant to cure antisemitism, has itself become its leading cause: the hatred simply follows the Jews whether they have a country or not.
Lavan's sheep were not ordinary property: they held the souls of the Dor HaMabul, the Dor Haflagah and Sedom, numbering 600,000, which Yaakov redeemed and which became the Jews who left Mitzrayim.
Before Matan Torah the tzaddikim could build their own 'switches' for the upper lights; Yaakov's peeled stripes on the rods were his way of fulfilling the mitzvah of tefillin, not a trick.
Esav did not chase Yaakov at Lavan's house because Lavan, the merkava of the Samech-Mem, was a greater danger than Esav himself; only Hashem's protection saved Yaakov there.
Yaakov's years with Lavan are a mirror of all of golus: Jews bring prosperity to their hosts and are accused of being parasites, as in the libels against Jewish finance ministers.

The Mashgiach reconciles the Targum's 'latecomers' with Rashi's 'expelled by the cloud': both are true, since Hashem rejects no Jew, but their own tardiness at the call to travel left them outside the camp's protection.

Rashi chose Kriyas Yam Suf and the war of Amalek because each showed Hashem's love for latecomers: a private splitting of the sea for Dasan and Aviram, and eternal anger at Amalek for attacking the stragglers. This is what gave Yisro the courage to come late.
Parshas Zachor is the one portion Hashem Himself requires to be read from the Torah, not Shema and not the Ten Commandments, and its message is how much Hashem cares for Jews who seem rejected.
Parshas Yisro is a second Matan Torah for latecomers: it is read long after Shavuos, opens with the story of a convert who came late, and the sefarim say the light of Shavuos comes down on it.

The two Haftaros mirror the two paths: Yechezkel, on Shavuos, reaches the vision through four barriers and in a place of purity by a river; Yeshaya, on Yisro, sees Hashem in the first passuk, in a year of impurity when King Uziyahu was a metzora.
The vav added to Yeser's name, which forms Yisro, is the vav of attachment: a vav is a nail, shaped like one, and like the hooks of the Mishkan's pillars it joins two things into one.

According to the Midrash the Mashgiach brings, Amalek's 'karcha' means he cooled them off: he got into the stragglers' hearts and told them they did not deserve to be Jews, killing their fervor before killing them.

The eternal war of Hashem with Amalek is a measure of His love for sinners: Amalek is punished for all generations precisely because he attacked Jews who had served idols and been spat out of the clouds.

The silver hooks of the pillars, which protrude beyond the curtains of the Mishkan, stand for the Jews at the borderline, and the word for their bands, 'chashukeihem', hints that these Jews are cherished by Hashem.

Rabbi Akiva, whose name contains 'eikev', the heel, is the soul of the lowest level of Klal Yisrael and the head of Torah she'baal peh in golus, so it was his soul that reminded Moshe of the forgotten Jews.
The lower and more distant a Jew is from Torah and mitzvos, the more reason he has to rejoice on Purim, since Purim proves that Hashem remembers him.

Since only twelve combinations of the Shem Havayah exist, matching twelve months and twelve tribes, Adar Sheni stands outside like the Jews outside the camp, and it was for such Jews that the miracle of Purim came.

The 3,550 Jews beyond the 600,000 are the 'forgotten' Jews: their silver did not go into the adanim, which bear Hashem's name, but into hooks that jutted outside the holiness of the Mishkan, where a tamei person may touch them.
The word adanim contains Hashem's name of Adnus, and the hundred adanim are the root of the hundred brachos said each day.
The hooks are called vavim because a vav joins one word to the next; so the Jews outside the camp, the Jews of Adar Sheni, remain connected to it.
Because the thirteenth month has no combination of Hashem's four-letter name and the Megillah never names Him, Adar Sheni is the special Purim of Jews in whom Hashem cannot be seen.
Moshe forgot the extra silver because the souls at the end of the Torah, like its last eight pesukim, belong to forgetting; Rabbi Akiva, whose root is beyond forgetting, could remind him.
Haman paid ten thousand talents only for the 600,000, not for the extra 3,550, because he made Amalek's mistake of thinking those Jews are rejected and not part of Klal Yisrael.
The double hiding of 'haster astir' describes our generation: the son not only cannot see his father but does not even know his father is there.

Counting 'by the number of names' is a count that keeps both sides: a name is individuality and a number is the collective, and Moshe's count joined each Jew's individual self to his being part of the whole.

The sages were called soferim not because they could count letters, which anyone can do, but because each letter was for them a davar shebeminyan, a counted thing that is never nullified, since they knew what each letter stands for.
The five camps correspond to the five Chumashim, with the Kohanim and Levi'im in the center just as Vayikra, Toras Kohanim, stands in the middle of the Torah.
The 22,000 Levi'im correspond to the 22 letters of the aleph-beis, the roots of the 600,000 letters, multiplied by a thousand, 'elef', which goes back to the aleph.
The megadef had to be evicted from the camp of Dan because the camp was a Sefer Torah, and adding a letter that does not belong renders a Sefer Torah pasul.
A line of a Sefer Torah, whose width the Gemara sets at three times the word for 'families', is a neighborhood of three Jewish families, and each word is a family.
Moshe's blessing that Levi will teach Torah is still visible: Kohanim and Levi'im are about a tenth of a congregation, yet well over half of the teachers of Torah.
Families, neighborhoods and communities correspond to the Torah's words, columns and sedras: people live together because their letters stood together in the Sefer Torah.
The custom of combined sedras is a calendar-wide demonstration of ahavas chinam, falling at the seasons connected to the churban, the hoped-for redemption and the students of Rabbi Akiva.

The Mashgiach maps the dispute over giving a Rav shlishi or shishi onto the Midrash in which the sea, created on the third day, refused to yield to man, created on the sixth, until it saw Yosef, who is shishi.
Even tzaddikim are not fully free of kinah, which is why one tzaddik traveled specially to Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz, who was free of it.
Yehuda and David are the moon and Ephraim stands opposite them, so the strife between Yehuda and Ephraim flows from the moon's diminution, and Yehonasan's love for David is a symbol of its repair.
A leap year itself carries the lesson of unity, because the extra month brings the moon and sun together, so in that year the Sefirah sedras need not be joined.
A Jew is like a switchboard: his mitzvos and aveiros register in all of creation, so removing kinah from his own heart removes it from the world.
The Mashgiach notes that Rabbi Akiva did not call emunah, the Ten Commandments or Shabbos 'the great rule of the Torah', but only 'love your fellow as yourself'.
A whole chevra, not only an individual, must say 'the world was created for us' and feel responsible to bring Moshiach.
Rachel's single act of sparing her sister shame achieved what the Akeidah and all the nisyonos of the Avos could not: it reversed the decree of exile.
Rachel did more than refrain from shaming Leah: she would not let Leah be shamed, and to prevent it she gave up her whole future with Yaakov.
Shaul merited kingship because he said his father would worry 'for us', counting his servant as an equal, just as Moshe said to his student 'choose for us'.
Mocking an ugly creature insults its Maker, as mocking a great artist's painting insults the artist.
The Mashgiach explains why shaming is punished more harshly than murder: precisely because the shamer does not feel he did anything terrible, he never comes to a broken heart and teshuvah.

He reads Boaz's failure to invite Manoach as an act meant for the sake of Heaven, to stir Manoach to daven harder, and still Boaz lost all his children, showing that good intentions do not permit shaming.

According to Rashi as the Mashgiach explains it, the exemptions of the newlywed and the planter of a vineyard exist mainly as cover, so that the soldier who returns because he fears his sins will not be recognized and shamed.

He explains that the chol bird's refusal to trouble Noach is the meaning of 'we will multiply like the chol' in Hamavdil: it refers to the bird, not to sand, and teaches that good middos bring eternal life.

Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin learned from the akeidah that the command to slaughter Yitzchak came from Hashem Himself while the command to stop came through an angel: to harm a Jew even an angel's word is not enough, but to save one even an angel is obeyed.

Rabbi Avraham of Slonim observed that a chain of great descendants, each great in his own right and not merely by inheritance, is the mark of the greatest leaders, and that Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin merited it for refusing to harm a Jew.

The Mashgiach explains that the shevatim, each corresponding to one of the months and to one of the twelve combinations of Hashem's Name, could not have acted wantonly; they ruled in beis din that Yosef was a rodef.

Following the Midrash, the Mashgiach explains that Adam had to eat from the Etz haDaas so that a yetzer hara and free choice would exist, and Moshe had to fail at Mei Merivah because had he entered Eretz Yisroel no galus would have been possible.
Since the brothers held Yosef liable to death, by sending everyone out and standing alone with them Yosef risked his life, choosing danger over shaming them.

Intending the sake of Heaven is not enough: Potifar's wife also meant it for Heaven's sake, yet she is a rasha because of her bad middos, while Tamar's willingness to die rather than shame Yehuda made the difference.

The Sanzer Rav's proof: when the Jews in Egypt lacked mitzvos they were given the blood of the Pesach and of the milah; had ruining an unworthy Jew been a mitzvah, they would have had plenty, burying those who died in the darkness.

Hashem's command to remember what Amalek did, rather than Israel's doubt, is like the king who blames the biting dog so as not to tell his friend he stole; Israel was meant to understand the hint by themselves.

The Mashgiach brings a remez that 've'ahavta es Hashem' and 've'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha ani Hashem' are equal in gematria: loving a Jew is loving Hashem, and hating a Jew is a sign that one does not love Hashem.

In the Slabodka story the Mashgiach sees the bachur's childlessness, despite his becoming a gadol, as the punishment for publicly exposing a friend, showing that being right about a stolen chiddush does not justify shaming him.
A man who did full teshuvah before his death was still kept out of Gan Eden for one forgotten act of embarrassing a chassan, which he never asked forgiveness for.
Reb Akiva Eiger preferred that his own father-in-law think he could not learn, at the risk of losing the shidduch, rather than cause another father-in-law distress over his chassan.
Reb Akiva Eiger let a strong kashya stand against his pilpul in public, revealing the answer only privately, because answering it would have lowered the local Rav in his own town.
Reb Yisrael Salanter held that the rabbanim of a generation are held responsible above for not teaching their communities good middos and not to shame others.
According to Reb Yisrael Salanter, asking forgiveness for lashon hara when it would only pain the victim is wrong; one should rather bear the punishment oneself than cause the other distress.
The Mashgiach presents stories of tzaddikim as a remedy for the weak emunah of the generation before Moshiach, citing tzaddikim who said that simply talking about a tzaddik already brings emunah.
In Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan's story, his refusal to reveal one poor man's name is what allowed a second, hidden poor man to trust him and ask for help.
Rabbi Shmuel Salant traced the young baal tokea's failure to a single proud thought that he could blow while the old man could not.
Rabbi Yosef Yoizel was won over not by Rabbi Yisrael Salanter's mussar talk itself but by seeing him interrupt it for a wagon driver's feelings.
Rabbi Yoizel argued that a man who claims he would give up Olam Haba to shame someone, but would not give up any Olam Hazeh, shows only how little Olam Haba is worth to him.
The Chofetz Chaim read 'az panim l'Gehinom' as a statement about teshuvah: every sinner can repent, but brazenness creates a presumption that he will not.
Rav Yosef Chaim's question to every visitor about the Kosel was a way of protecting the honor of a guest: it showed that people came to Yerushalayim for the Kosel and only stopped by him on the way.
The Mashgiach contrasts the tzaddik with an ordinary person: the tzaddik's thought, even in his own illness, is not to trouble other Jews, while another thinks only of what he himself needs.
In the musaf, na'anuim and eruv stories, a tzaddik sets aside a rule or a mitzvah derabbanan for another person's feelings or honor; the Mashgiach presents each as the way a tzaddik weighs things.
Rav Chaim Ozer's answer distinguishes two obligations: illness exempted him from sukkah, but not from hachnasas orchim, just as Avraham Avinu sat waiting for guests while in pain after his milah.
The Mashgiach reads the Gemara's 'aliba d'Abaye', 'according to Abaye', literally as 'according to Abaye's heart': a sage holds his view because his heart, from the root of his soul, tells him so.
From the grammar rule that a verb ending in nun drops it as a noun, the Mashgiach derives that from aman, to believe, comes em, mother: emunah comes from the mother.

The seder's three matzos, from grain that brings intellect, stand for the Avos, and its four cups of wine, which bring out feeling, stand for the Imahos, like the three-headed and four-headed shin on the two sides of the tefillin.
A father who breaks in to his son's house without knowing it is his son's still would not harm him, because his heart knows; so too a Jew's bond to Hashem works beneath conscious knowledge.
Eisav concluded that he lost the berachos because of his wives, never imagining the fault was his own, the same rationalization as the fox and the grapes.

According to the Avnei Nezer as the Mashgiach brings it, a woman may rely on a single witness about her husband's death because she feels whether he is alive; her believing the witness is itself the sign.
The Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his unaware father shows that the bond of feeling works even without knowledge, and the Mashgiach reads the Jew's bond to Hashem the same way.
Matters of fact are the same for every mind, but in matters open to opinion the heart decides according to the root of a person's soul; thus a ruling 'according to Abaye's heart' reflects his nature.

Grain builds the intellect while wine weakens it but strengthens feeling; so the Seder pairs three matzos with the Avos and four cups with the Imahos, and the tefillin carry a three-headed shin and a four-headed shin.
The word emunah itself shows that faith comes from the mother: a verb ending in nun loses that nun when it becomes a noun, so amun becomes em.
Esav married Yishmael's daughter because he concluded from the brachos he lost that his wives were at fault, the same 'sour grapes' self-justification born of gaavah.

There is no true Jewish apikorus: his denial is a rationalization to permit his desires, as shown by the woman who asked a newspaper to stop reporting miracles so she could go to the beach on Shabbos.
The rare arrangement of the year, with Parshas Balak read now, is hashgachah pratis: its message of curse turned to blessing is what Jews need at this time.
Bilaam's claims may have been justified, yet Hashem refused even to hear them; the refusal itself expresses His love.
Hashem's love is that of a father to his beloved child, an unearned love, flowing from the attribute of chesed alone.
The navi's 'remember' is a plea that a Jew not lose the feeling of closeness and think there is a separation between him and Hashem because of his hardships.
No sin offering is brought on Shabbos, unlike the festivals, because Shabbos is a day of love, in which 'love covers all sins'.
The Mashgiach reads the world's constant preoccupation with so small a people as itself a sign of the Jews' unique place.
He turns a worsening situation on its head: getting worse and worse means getting better and better.
The pesukim the children told Mordechai in his time of danger are, for the Mashgiach, a present-day source of emunah against the nations' schemes.
Other peoples' claims to be the best are simply laughed at; only the Jews' claim to be chosen provokes the nations, because they know in their hearts that it is true.

Since the nations cannot themselves become Jews and accept the Torah, their recognition turns into jealousy, and jealousy into hatred, as with Yosef's brothers; this is the root of the persecutions of the exile.

The admissions of Mark Twain, Tolstoy and President Adams are themselves a fulfillment of the pesukim that the nations will call Israel wise and will walk by its light; those gentiles with a point of truth concede it.
Spain, once the mightiest nation, sank into insignificance after it expelled its Jews, showing that the nations' greatness came from Jewish minds.
The Torah's warning that the land would be desolate is also a guarantee: for two thousand years no other people could settle it, and it flourishes only when the Jews return.
The Mashgiach sees the change in Eretz Yisroel within a few decades, from desolation to fruitfulness and wealth, as the Gemara's revealed sign of the end, a wonder seen with one's own eyes.
The Mashgiach reads 'and they did not rebel against His word' as praise of the Jews: during choshech they could have walked out of a paralyzed Egypt, but they stayed because Moshe told them to wait.

Those who died during the darkness were the wealthy and the 'intelligentsia' close to the government, who did not want to leave; the bnei Efrayim who left early failed for lack of emunas chachamim, not even asking Amram.
Rebuke suits a strong generation, as in Yeshayahu's time; Malachi, the last prophet, speaks to the broken generation before Moshiach, so he opens with 'I have loved you'.
Hashem calling Klal Yisrael 'mother' is like a grandmother who calls the baby 'mamele' out of love, and the mitzvos even of the simplest Jews become pearls in Hashem's crown.
Hashem says 'Bo', come, rather than 'go', because He goes along with Moshe: like a mother who goes with her child into a dark room, Hashem is with a Jew even in a place of impurity.
Yehudah married right after the sale of Yosef because, having lost all his worlds, he chose to begin from the beginning; this is the lesson of the first mitzvos of the Torah.
The Mashgiach reads the parallel of time, place and soul so literally that he can say Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and every Jew are each 'a Yid', while Sunday and America are 'a goy'.
Because the inner side of Eretz Yisrael is the Jewish soul, the land is not an object used for a mitzvah like tzitzis; the land itself is the one that keeps the mitzvah, and its mitzvah is Shabbos.
Not only do Jews need Eretz Yisrael; the land needs Jews, just as Shabbos needs Jews, and this is why the tochachah ends with the remembrance of the land.

Forcing the Torah at Sinai was a greater honor than accepting it by choice: what comes by choice is a level that can be lost, while what is necessary, like life itself, is eternal, as with a woman taken by force who may never be sent away.

Korbanos can atone only because sin is incidental to a Jew: ink poured into water becomes one with it, but dirt on a person or a diamond comes off, and Avraham's question at the bris bein habesarim was answered with exactly this.
Yirmiyahu's question about buying a field on the eve of the churban is the same as Avraham's 'bameh eida', and both are answered by the same principle that sin is only incidental to Jews.
The Torah was given in the desert and not in Eretz Yisrael as a comfort for all generations: when Jews cannot come to their root, the root comes to them, just as Har Moriah came to Har Sinai.

The message that the Jews' good is essential was given through Bilam precisely because a concession from the adversary, like the yetzer hara forced to answer amen at the Shabbos table, is the greatest praise.
The chachamim's reduction of forty lashes to thirty-nine expresses the Oral Torah's knowledge that the first of a Jew's forty days of formation never sinned.
The Written Torah records the curses of Ki Savo and the Oral Torah the blessings, because blessing belongs to the Oral Torah, the kallah that is the source of blessing.
Parah adumah is called a chok, though it atones for the egel, so that accusers who ask its reason in order to recall the sin are answered that it is beyond understanding.
In the Holy of Holies, full of gold, there is no reminder of the egel, because at the innermost place the love for Yisrael shows that there was never a sin.
Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, the fortieth day on which the Oral Torah came down, is the 'fortieth lash' that the Oral Torah does not give, and so it is truly a consolation.
The melave malka belongs to David HaMelech because it alone nourishes the luz bone, untouched by Adam's sin, and David, the tikkun of Adam, is 'chai vekayam'; hence its link to techiyas hameisim.
Sefer Bereishis tells of the creation of the point of Klal Yisrael in the Avos, and Sefer Shemos of its spreading out into the twelve tribes, each with his own strength.

Since the Torah gives no reason for Avraham's choosing, his point comes from the Divine will alone, and therefore it cannot be lost through a person's choices; milah at eight days, done without the child's consent, expresses this.
Shabbos, fixed by Hashem's will and not dependent on beis din, is a day of will like the point of Avraham, which does not depend on anything a person does.
The maftir, an eighth aliyah that rereads what was already read, reflects techiyas hameisim and the eighth level of Moshiach, which is why it is followed by the berachah of 'Magen David'.
The vav before 'Tidal' hints that joining is the essence of Edom, the present exile, whose kiss is worse than a bite.
The Haggadah proves Yaakov came only to sojourn from his sons' words to Pharaoh, because Yaakov's way to avoid sinking in Egypt was to have them declare openly that they did not belong there.

The feminine 'merivah' in Avraham's words, against the masculine 'riv' of the narrative, shows that between Avraham and Lot there was only a weak, small dispute, while among the shepherds it became a forceful quarrel.
The Mashgiach reads the dispute between Avraham and Lot as a halachic question: whether Hashem's promise of the land to Avraham had already taken effect or would only take effect later.
Rabbi Zechariah and the Chachamim did not disagree in halachah but in assessing the situation: whether offering a blemished animal would lead people to a false halachah.
Avraham's change from zealotry in Ur Kasdim to peace in Eretz Yisrael followed from his mission: once promised a following, he was no longer allowed to risk his life, because his students needed him.
The vav that the Midrash says belongs to Tidal's name is a 'vav of joining': the fourth kingdom torments the Jews by joining with them, as Esav bit Yaakov with a kiss.
Unlike the earlier kingdoms, each of which was one nation, the fourth kingdom, 'Tidal king of nations', is many peoples united under one church with one policy toward the Jews.
The Mashgiach reads the placement of the goral verse between the two commands to drive out the nations as a statement that a land held by Hashem's lot cannot be shared with the nations.
He shows from the dual meaning of the root (yerushah, to inherit; horashah, to drive out), like 'saklu me'even', that the inheritance bond is one that cannot be cut off.
A fashion designer creates a new style because his nation's angel above dresses that way, which is why the laws of dress are part of the laws of avodah zarah.
Moshe recognized from the very sound of the shouting at the egel that it was avodah zarah, not war; the Mashgiach applies this to the frenzied shouting of ball games.
The Arizal, the soul of sod, passed away in the Nine Days, because these days, like his teaching, hold a hidden good whose time to be revealed has not yet come.
Dovid HaMelech swam alone in deep waters, and a tzaddik passes trials so that his followers need not; in our generation one must have a 'buddy'.
Citing the Eretz Tzvi, he explains that Jerusalem fell over Kamtza because a son reveals his father's inner self: Kamtza's son's hatred showed Kamtza was a friend only outwardly.
The Mashgiach locates the turning point of Yosef's rise in his love for others: he noticed the sad faces of Pharaoh's two servants and cared enough to ask.
Yosef's concealment is read as a hidden yichud: like the silent Shemoneh Esrei that must precede the loud repetition, the gathering of the shevatim in Egypt had to stay secret until it was complete.
Through the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'there is none as wise as you', the Mashgiach teaches that one can only understand someone from above him, so we cannot judge tzaddikim.
A tzaddik's persecution of another can be a hidden kindness: by an explanation the Mashgiach cites, the Ropshitzer's harsh opposition spared the Lentshner from heavier judgment in heaven.
The Mashgiach treats yiras shamayim as a faculty of perception: the Mechaber demands it of a shochet not as piety alone but as what lets his fingers feel a fine nick.

On the ninth of Teves, the Mashgiach explains that Ezra 'died a second time' when Klal Yisrael lost the sensitivity behind his takanah, as Rav Ada bar Ahava tore kriah again for Rav when his teaching was found missing.
An owner pays for his animal's damage because, as the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches, his property is an extension of his soul; the damage reveals a flaw in himself.
Through ahavas Yisroel a person becomes a partner in every mitzvah another Jew does, so mitzvos he cannot do himself are still completed in him and his limbs can rise at techiyas hameisim.
Hashem does not carry out a judgment on a person until the person has pronounced it on himself, which is why judging others harshly is so dangerous.
The order of davening, in the morning and at night, puts Hashem's love for Yisroel before the command to love Hashem, showing that ahavas Yisroel is the introduction to ahavas Hashem.

Each kaddish in davening is a staircase between the worlds; between Beriah and Shemoneh Esrei there is none because one may not interrupt between Ga'al Yisroel and Shemoneh Esrei, and after Shemoneh Esrei there is a kaddish on the way back down.
Unlike every war since Yehoshua's conquest, in which Jews suffered first, this war is good for the Jews, because the enemy aims to destroy Eretz Yisroel, matching the Apter Rav's prediction.
Emes, the last of Krias Shema's 248 words, matches the heel, so the generation of the heel before Moshiach is the one charged with emes.
The word emes is not written in the Torah's parsha of Shema; we add it ourselves, hinting that the last generation must itself supply the truth.
Without emes, divine service loses its life: remove the aleph of emes and only 'mes', death, remains.
Truth is by nature one, like the single correct time on a clock; a multitude of competing 'truths' is itself the sign of falsehood foretold for the end of days.
Treating one's chassidus like a sports team, to feel great through the group, is the pride the Steipler describes, and the very opposite of chassidus.
Different chassidic paths are like the twelve tribes with their twelve gates: legitimate differences of root, which must not become hatred.
A bad thought about a fellow Jew is worse than bad speech, because thought reaches higher worlds; by the same measure a good thought about him does more good than good speech.
Ten Jews joined as a tzibbur are not ten individuals but a new entity with a collective soul, which is why a tzibbur can say Kedushah and read the Torah, something no single tzaddik can do.
The bond that makes a zimun is created by eating together: three who ate separately and then meet cannot bench with a zimun.
'Yachdav' means bound, not merely together: as with shaatnez, wool and linen lying loosely one on the other are not 'yachdav'.

Not believing in techiyas hameisim is not punished by losing it but is a symptom of having no share in it; likewise Ammon and Moav's not bringing bread and water was a sign that they have no connection to Klal Yisrael.
Each exile struck in another dimension: Bavel in breadth, Yavan in height against the Shechinah (the fifteen amos), and Edom also in time, an exile without an end (the hundred and fifty days).

The thirty letters of a line in a Sefer Torah are learned from the korban Pesach and not from Noach's families leaving the teivah, because there the group was breaking up while at the Pesach it was gathering into one chaburah.
Amalek, the klipah of 'reishis', concentrates on beginnings, so a new beis medrash and a new effort in tefillah meet the strongest opposition.
Like a patient for whom orange juice is at the moment more important than bread, in the days before Moshiach tefillah takes first place without lessening the greatness of Torah study.
Many small daily sacrifices of one's wishes add up to a mesiras nefesh greater even than the one great act of giving up life.
Eating and farbrenging together in the shtibel after davening is no interruption of tefillah but can itself lead to accepting the yoke of Heaven.
The differences of nusach and custom between Jewish groups reflect the twelve gates in heaven, one for each shevet, which is why the Torah says to appoint judges 'for your tribes'.
When Providence draws certain people together as friends, it shows they share a root of the soul, and the love between them must be stronger.
The Mashgiach reads the seven haftaros of consolation as a dialogue: for six weeks the navi consoles and Klal Yisrael is silent, and only in the seventh does she answer Hashem herself, as a bride.
Following the Maharal, the two middle handbreadths of the luchos, held by neither Hashem nor Moshe, were the partnership itself between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like two who hold a garment together.

A wife's bond can be ended by divorce, a daughter's cannot be cut but her father can be angry, while a mother's love for her infant cannot be weakened at all; Hashem calls Klal Yisrael 'my mother', the love of the mother to her child.

Like a hospital with its own generator, when the calf severed the bond of groom and bride, the higher bond of 'my daughter' and 'my mother' remained as a backup, so the calf could be forgotten while Sinai was not.

The Amora's unusual sharpness against anyone who says terumah can be redeemed is explained because Klal Yisrael is Hashem's terumah: the claim that Hashem exchanged the Jews for another nation is Bilaam's view.
Yom Kippur equals 'rotzeh ani' in gematria: it is the day when each Jew's inner will to do Hashem's will comes out.

Ending the Torah on Simchas Torah with 'l'einei kol Yisrael', the breaking of the luchos that brought forgetting, and beginning Bereishis at once shows that the forgetting does not reach Klal Yisrael, for whom the world was created.

A man with free choice is a greater danger than a king, whose heart is in Hashem's hand; this is why the Gemara stresses that Haman was 'a man and not a king', and the Mashgiach illustrates it with saving someone from a man versus from a pit.

The 'waters' in the kapitel are forces of judgment, and the power of the splitting of the Yam Suf, when all the world's waters split, is eternal: every flood that threatens the Jews still splits before them.
Pre-war America was like Pisom and Raamses: whatever was built sank into the ground and had to be built again, and so the immigrants' Yiddishkeit sank into the 'clay' of America.
A bird caught in a trap escapes only by breaking a leg or a wing, but here 'the trap broke and we escaped': the Jews came out whole, as seen in the rebirth after the war.
'Maker of heaven and earth' in the present tense means Hashem constantly creates new heavens and earth, and in the new heavens a decree that was written may no longer be written.
Har Tziyon was a marker that left the imprint of G-dliness on the world; after its destruction, the Jews who trust in Hashem take over its function among the nations.
Just as, according to the Rambam, Yerushalayim's holiness from the Shechinah outlasts every conquest, the holiness of a Jew from the Shechinah cannot be taken away by the nations or by sin.

Aharon's life was the Beis Hamikdash: his 123 years correspond to the Mishkan's thirty, twenty and ten amos, from the outer view to the Kodesh Hakodashim, so his passing on Rosh Chodesh Av is the root of Tisha B'Av.
Joining two parshiyos on one Shabbos is itself a tikkun for baseless hatred, which is why it happens only at the times of geulah or of repairing the churban.
Since all souls form one rope from top to bottom, a weakening of simple Jews' emunah can pull down the chassid's chassidus, and the reverse is equally true.
Kamtza and Bar Kamtza could have saved Yerushalayim with a handshake and a l'chaim, because two individuals making peace can tip a whole city.
The kingship of Yehuda and Moshiach came through Yehuda's refinement in not reclaiming his pledge from Tamar, not through his piety alone.
Av corresponds to Shimon, the tribe of 'hearing'; when Aharon passed, the 'hearing', the bond of togetherness, went into galus to the Kenaani.

The Mashgiach reads Hashem's answer to Avraham, 'in the merit of korbanos', as a proof about the Jewish essence: if a korban can wipe away a Jew's sin, his sin is only incidental, so his children must return to Eretz Yisrael.
A Jew who sins is like a man who fell into black mud: soap and water restore him, whereas for a man with dark skin no scrubbing helps, for the color is his essence.
Eretz Yisrael is 'a Jew in geography': everything that belongs to a Jewish soul belongs to the Jewish place, which is why it spits out sinners just as the Jewish soul spits out evil.

Yosef's goblet, 'gevia', hints at the three levels: gimmel for the three avos, beis-yud for the twelve shevatim, ayin for the seventy souls; once the seventy existed, the family could go down to Mitzrayim.

Pesach determines the weekday of Tisha b'Av because a Jewish churban is always rooted in geulah; the Mashgiach says a time will come when Tisha b'Av will be perhaps the most beautiful Yom Tov of the year.

Serach, who brought Yaakov the news that Yosef lived, took on the quality of Eliyahu, who is appointed over good news; she is thus 'two' and completes the seventy, hinting that redemption already walks with the Jews into galus.
The Gemara (Yocheved) and the Midrash (Serach) do not argue: Yocheved is the root of the redeemer Moshe, Serach carries Eliyahu who announces the geulah, and both say that galus begins with geulah.
Refidim is read as 'perud', separation: Amalek's power came from the lack of unity, so the teshuvah that Rashi says they did on leaving Refidim was their becoming one before Sinai.
Citing tzaddikim, the Mashgiach says that when two Jews come together they form Hashem's Name, written with two yuds.
Nearing Sinai without the Torah was already a gift: the unity of Rosh Chodesh was the klal of the Torah, and the giving of the Torah on Shavuos brought only its particulars.
Because the darkness of the later generations is greater, Hashem lights greater lamps, as seen in the growing revelations from Rashbi to the Arizal to the Ba'al Shem Tov.
At the level of the fiftieth day, 'one' is not the smallest number but the only one; that is why the fiftieth day, like the Levi'im, is not counted.

The Aron taking no space, bowing with room in the Azarah, and finding lodging in Yerushalayim are one miracle at three levels: the closer to the Kodesh HaKodashim, the less it is even a miracle, since there heaven's nature rules.
Moshe Rabbeinu, called the shofar of Klal Yisrael, was above time and could move the day of Matan Torah; 'Vayedaber Moshe es mo'adei Hashem' means he carries the festivals to the Jews each year.
The students of Rabbi Akiva lacked respect all year, but were punished in Sefirah because these are the days designated for refining middos before receiving the Torah.
The Torah does not reveal which tree was the Etz HaDa'as so that the tree should not be shamed, showing Hashem's care for the honor even of a plant.

The juxtaposed parshiyos of Tamar and Potiphar's wife describe the origins of the two Moshiachs, and both women acted for Heaven; only good middos separated them, so one merited and the other did not.
One who takes his own life has no atonement because death, which normally atones, is itself the sin; yet Tamar chose death over shaming Yehudah, so shaming is graver than suicide.
The word panim reflects that the face is a window to the inside: each face differs because each character differs, so one may no more resent another's opinions than his face.
A Kohen does not bless 'who did not make me a Yisrael', since that would be gaining honor through the disgrace of other Jews whose ancestors sinned at the Golden Calf.
The Torah lists the pig's kosher sign before its disqualifying one, opening even with a compliment to an impure animal.
The Mashgiach reads the Maharal on Kamtza as a lesson that one who stands beside a baal machlokes as his friend and ally shares in the churban, even if he did nothing himself.

He explains R' Sholom of Belz's acrostic on the word 'frummer', and contrasts the 'frummer' who brushes off a broken-hearted person before Ne'ilah with the erlicher Yid who listens, since that is a chessed.

He sees the practices of the baal korei reading for everyone and of singing at a hakafah of yichus as built on the same principle as the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av: one who can do more must still follow the custom, so as not to expose those who cannot.
From R' Yisrael Salanter's last night the Mashgiach learns that a person's final moment reflects his whole life: the tzaddik spent it sparing another Jew from fear, which shows what his life was.

On the Mishnah 'the brazen go to Gehinnom', the Mashgiach explains that every sinner can do teshuvah, but the brazen never does, so he has a one-way road; this is why the Chofetz Chaim would not keep the insolent bochur.
R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld weighed comforting a widow by letting her son lead Mussaf as a greater honor for the congregation than the rule about who should lead.
The Mashgiach reads ordinary courtesies, such as a visible house number or a phone number said slowly, as continuing Hashem's own middas hachesed, which can sweeten a decree on the one who does them.
Singing in the middle of a chasan's drasha, which a capable bochur may resent, is presented as a deliberate chesed for the chasan who cannot speak.

Through the mashal of an ink stain, the Mashgiach explains that a blemish ignored on a sack is a real flaw on a silk shirt; so a tzaddik is held to account for indirectly causing shame even when his psak was correct.
R' Akiva Eiger preferred to step down from the bimah seemingly without an answer rather than show the rav of the city that his kushya was no kushya.

On 'az panim l'Gehinom', the Mashgiach explains that teshuvah helps for every sin, but the Mishnah knows a brazen person will not do teshuvah, which is why the insolent bochur was sent away while the one who sinned was kept.
Giving slightly less than requested, or bargaining over a price, can itself be a chesed, so that the other person does not regret having asked too little.
The Mashgiach reads 'all Jews are sons of kings' through the hidden virtue: since each Jew has something no other Jew has, in that respect he is a king over all of them.

Just as each Jew corresponds to a letter of the Torah and the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, each Jew has a sod part, the hidden virtue, which is why Rabbi Shimon, the revealer of the Torah's secrets, is the one who reveals it.
The sin of Rabbi Akiva's students is understood as failing to honor the other's hidden virtue, even when one is truly greater in learning and yiras Shamayim; Rabbi Shimon's revelation undid that.

The Mashgiach links Lag Ba'omer to parshas Behar, read around that time: the shemitah of the land shows that the Shabbos reaches the earth, the lowest element, just as Rabbi Shimon reaches the lowliest Jews.
In the Zohar's words at Rabbi Shimon's passing, the earth may not be proud that all return to it, since Rabbi Shimon is not consumed by it; his aspect rules over the earth.
The Mashgiach reads matanos la'evyonim in light of 'there is no poverty except in da'as': the main poor one Hashem gives to is the one poor in understanding.
The very absence of da'as at a bris is its beauty: the infant who understands nothing is bound to the hidden root of Avraham Avinu, something a later, conscious act could not achieve in the same way.
The joy of Purim is the joy of a Jew at the point he does not feel: like an eight-day-old at his bris, one rejoices with the hidden love present in every Jew.

Milah, given without da'as at eight days, and tefillin, given with da'as at thirteen, are two sides of one bond, and Purim, whose 'sasson' is milah and 'yekar' is tefillin, joins them up to the peak of 'ad d'lo yada'.
Since 'the king' in the Megillah means the Ribono shel Olam, the decree to bow to Haman came from Hashem, and its whole purpose was to bring out Mordechai's mesiras nefesh from the hidden root.
Teves is to time what Mitzrayim is to place: both are the domain of darkness and hester panim, so Yaakov's descent to Mitzrayim in Parshas Vayigash is the model for entering Teves.
Chanukah falls at the head of Teves so that its light crushes the 'head' of the month, and its power extends through the whole month, as Rosh Chodesh includes the whole month.
The 'visions of the night' in which Hashem spoke to Yaakov correspond to the long nights of Teves, and the doubled 'Yaakov, Yaakov' is a language of love spoken precisely on the threshold of exile.
Chanukah is called a beloved mitzvah because it exists to show Jews that Hashem loves them, just as they are about to enter the darkness of Teves.
Hallel means to illuminate, so the last Hallel of Chanukah is meant to light up the whole of nature in hard times.

The Mashgiach reads Targum Yonasan's night journey to Yerushalayim and back as Hashem first showing the Jews where they truly belong, then sending them back to reach it through their own work, like a king's son who must still go through his training.
He compares the Korban Pesach's leap over levels to dancing: in a dance one jumps higher than one really is.

The second of Sivan is not a commemoration: since the Torah is eternal, every year each Jewish soul again declares 'na'aseh', even if the body does not hear it, just as the Arizal describes souls acting at night without the person knowing.

Since each Jewish soul belongs to a letter of Hashem's Sefer Torah, a missing soul would make the whole Torah invalid; this is why every Jew must come to his tikkun, and he links it to the Shavuos custom of bringing all the Sifrei Torah.

Boaz's mention of 'vinegar' was not discouraging talk to a convert but comfort: even the 'vinegar' from her line, Menashe, would become the teacher of all Israel, since every hamotzi follows his halachah.

The place 'baked first' is chosen for the brachah not because it is the best piece but because it shows Hashem's plan that this part reach its tikkun first; so the halachah of a soul whose own way was through tikkun came through Menashe.
He reads the melachos of bread in Hilchos Shabbos as the stages of tikkun after Adam's sin, with baking as the final stage after which the bread is ready for a brachah.
